paragraphs: Moby Dick, published in 1851, is Herman Melville's mighty reckoning with obsession. Melville himself had shipped out on a whaling vessel as a young man and spent years among sailors, harpooneers, and cannibals of the South Seas. He poured everything he knew, and everything he feared, into the story of the Pequod, a whaling ship commanded by a monomaniac captain hunting a white whale across the world's oceans. When it appeared, the book was a failure. Readers wanted adventure stories; Melville gave them philosophy, cetology, metaphysics, and doom. It sold a few thousand copies and was forgotten.

It took seventy years for the world to catch up. In the 1920s, critics rediscovered Moby Dick and recognized it as perhaps the greatest American novel ever written: a vast, strange, magnificent book that contains multitudes. It is at once a detailed manual of the whaling industry, a gallery of unforgettable characters, a meditation on God and nature and evil, and a tragedy of Shakespearean scale. At its center stands Captain Ahab, one of literature's great monomaniacs, and the white whale, Moby Dick, who may be an animal, or fate, or God, or nothing at all.

The story is told by Ishmael, the sole survivor, a young wanderer who signs aboard the Pequod seeking escape and finds instead a voyage into the heart of darkness. What follows here are the essential passages: the famous opening, the friendship with Queequeg, the sermon, the terrible chapter on whiteness, Ahab's oath, and the final three-day chase that ends in one of the most devastating finales in all of literature.

Melville knew the world he described because he had lived it. As a young man of twenty-one he shipped out on the whaler Acushnet and spent eighteen months at sea, deserted in the Marquesas, lived among islanders, served on other vessels, and came home with a head full of stories. He wrote Moby Dick in a fever of inspiration on a Massachusetts farm, in sight of a mountain he called the whale's hump, reading Shakespeare and corresponding with his friend Nathaniel Hawthorne, to whom the book is dedicated. He put everything into it: his adventures, his reading, his doubts about God, his rage at fate. The public did not want it. He died in 1891, largely forgotten, working as a customs inspector. The masterpiece had to wait for another century to find its readers.
chapters.title: About This Book

paragraphs: Few sentences in literature are more famous than the three words that open this novel. "Call me Ishmael." With that quiet introduction, the narrator steps forward: not a hero, not a captain, just a young man with a restless soul and an empty purse, asking to be known by a borrowed biblical name, the name of the outcast son of Abraham, the wanderer.

"Some years ago — never mind how long precisely — having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world." That is how Ishmael explains himself, with a shrug that covers a deep melancholy. Whenever he finds himself growing grim about the mouth, whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in his soul, whenever he feels like knocking people's hats off in the street, he knows it is time to get to sea as soon as he can.

He describes the feeling with unforgettable precision. Whenever he finds himself growing grim about the mouth, whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in his soul, whenever he finds himself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses and bringing up the rear of every funeral he meets, then, he says, he knows it is high time to get to sea as soon as he can. It is a kind of spiritual hygiene, this urge, a recognition that the land, with its streets and shops and respectable hypocrisies, is slowly suffocating him. The ocean promises something the land cannot: vastness, danger, and truth.

This, Ishmael insists, is his substitute for pistol and ball. Going to sea is how he drives away his gloom. He does not go as a passenger, paying money to be carried like a parcel. He goes as a common sailor, before the mast, to feel the salt and the labour in his own body. There is something almost religious in his longing for the ocean, and something desperate too. The sea, for Ishmael, is the great cleanser, the place where a man can be scrubbed clean of the land's hypocrisies.

So he makes his way to New Bedford, the great whaling port of Massachusetts, with a whaling voyage in mind. It is December, cold and grey, and the town is full of sailors, missionaries, widows, and sharks of every kind. Ishmael takes a room at a shabby inn called the Spouter-Inn, and there, on a cold winter's night, he will meet the strangest and truest friend of his life. But first he must survive the night, for the inn is full, and the landlord has only one bed left to offer, and it is already occupied.
chapters.title: Call Me Ishmael

paragraphs: The bed's occupant turns out to be Queequeg, a harpooneer from the South Seas, a tattooed prince of the island of Kokovoko who has shipped out on whaling voyages to see the world. When Ishmael first sees him, in the dim light of the inn bedroom, he is terrified. Queequeg is a dark, tattooed savage, his whole body covered in strange blue markings, his head shaved bald except for a scalp-lock, calmly going through some heathen ritual with a little wooden idol before climbing into bed with a tomahawk pipe between his teeth.

Ishmael spends the night pressed against the wall, clutching his blanket, certain he will be murdered before dawn. But morning changes everything. Over breakfast, watching Queequeg's quiet dignity, his thoughtfulness, his simple honesty, Ishmael begins to feel ashamed of his fear. Here is a man, he realizes, more civilized in his soul than half the Christians of New Bedford. By the end of the day they are sharing the pipe of peace, and Queequeg, in his broken English and eloquent gestures, proposes that they become bosom friends, sworn brothers.

Queequeg has his own religion, and he practices it with a seriousness that puts Ishmael's casual Christianity to shame. He worships a little black wooden idol named Yojo, and when his holy days come he observes a strict fast, sitting motionless in his room from dawn to dusk in a kind of trance, neither eating nor speaking. Ishmael, watching him, is struck by the dignity of this devotion. He begins to wonder whether a man's worth lies in the name of his god or in the honesty of his heart, and he finds Queequeg's heart beyond reproach.

It is one of the most beautiful friendships in literature, and the most unlikely. Ishmael, the educated, melancholy white wanderer, and Queequeg, the tattooed pagan harpooneer, pledge themselves to each other with a solemn ritual, and from that moment they share everything: money, pipe, bed, and fate. Queequeg even gives Ishmael half his savings, pressing the money on him with a generosity that shames the careful selfishness of civilization.

Together they sign aboard the Pequod, a grim old whaling ship out of Nantucket, and Queequeg ships as harpooneer. The ship's owners, the shrewd Quaker captains Peleg and Bildad, are scandalized by the pagan at first, but Queequeg proves his worth by hurling a harpoon with impossible precision. As the Pequod sails out past the lighthouse on Christmas morning, Ishmael stands at the rail with his new brother beside him, and for the first time in years, the November in his soul begins to lift. He does not know yet what kind of captain waits below deck, or what white shadow haunts the captain's dreams.
chapters.title: Queequeg

paragraphs: Before they sail, on a cold Sunday morning, Ishmael slips into the Whaleman's Chapel in New Bedford, a little church full of memorial tablets to sailors lost at sea. The pulpit is the strangest he has ever seen: built high against the wall in the shape of a ship's prow, reached only by a rope ladder that the preacher draws up after him, as if cutting himself off from the world to speak to it.

The chapel is full of ghosts. Its walls are hung with marble tablets, each one carved with the name of a whaleman lost at sea, and the dates of his birth and death, and a few words of mourning. Ishmael reads them as he waits: young men of nineteen and twenty, taken by whales, by storms, by fever in foreign ports. The whole place breathes the shortness of a sailor's life and the nearness of death. It is the perfect antechamber to the story Melville is about to tell, for the Pequod too will soon add its own names to such a wall.

The preacher is Father Mapple, once a harpooneer himself, now a chaplain to whalemen, a massive old man with a voice like a storm. His text is the story of Jonah, the prophet who fled from God and was swallowed by the great fish, and his sermon is a masterpiece of sea-theology. He tells how Jonah, commanded to preach to Nineveh, took ship in the opposite direction, and how the storm rose, and how the sailors cast lots and found the guilty man, and how Jonah asked to be thrown into the sea.

Father Mapple's lesson is stern and simple, and it echoes through everything that follows. Woe to him who seeks to please rather than to appal. Woe to him who would not be true even though to be false were salvation. The sermon is about obedience to a higher command, about the terrible price of running from one's duty, about repentance in the belly of the whale. Ishmael listens, moved despite himself, and files the story away in his memory.

Neither Ishmael nor the reader can know, sitting in that little chapel, how the story of Jonah will return. But Melville has planted it like a seed. For the Pequod too will sail with a captain fleeing from every duty but his own vengeance, and the sea too will open its mouth, and the question of who is Jonah and who is the whale will haunt the voyage to its bitter end.
chapters.title: Father Mapple's Sermon
The Whiteness of the Whale
paragraphs: Of all the strange chapters in this strange book, none is stranger or more haunting than the one in which Ishmael tries to explain what it is about Moby Dick that fills him with dread. It is not the whale's size, though he is monstrous. It is not his ferocity, though he has destroyed ships and men. It is something else, something that has nothing to do with strength at all.

"It was the whiteness of the whale that above all things appalled me." White should be beautiful. White is the colour of purity, of brides and angels, of the ermine and the snow. And yet, Ishmael argues, there is a horror in whiteness too, a ghastly, spectral quality that chills the soul. He lists the evidence: the white albatross that haunts the southern seas, the white shark with its ghastly glare, the albino man whose very skin seems unnatural, the pallor of a corpse, the white shroud of the polar snows.

What is it that makes whiteness terrible? Ishmael circles the question like the whale circling a ship. Perhaps it is that white, having no colour of its own, takes on the colour of whatever it touches, and so seems false, empty, a mask. Perhaps it is that whiteness reminds us of the vast, blank indifference of the universe, the heartless voids and immensities that care nothing for man. Or perhaps, most terribly, whiteness is the visible sign of the unknown, the colour of a mystery that can never be solved.

For Ahab, the white whale is evil incarnate, the mask behind which all malice hides, and he will strike through the mask if it kills him. For Ishmael, the whiteness is more frightening still, because it may mean nothing at all. It may be that the universe is blank and senseless, that there is no meaning behind the mask, only the white, silent, indifferent deep. This chapter is the philosophical heart of the novel, and readers have argued about its meaning for more than a century. What is certain is that after reading it, you will never look at the colour white in quite the same way again.

Ishmael pushes the thought further, into darker water. He remembers that in many cultures white is the colour of mourning, of ghosts, of the shroud. He thinks of the great white albatross that follows ships through the southern ocean for days without rest, a living omen. He thinks of how the Arctic snows can blind a man and drive him mad with their endless sameness. And he arrives at the most disturbing idea of all: that whiteness is terrible precisely because it suggests a universe without meaning, a vast blankness behind which there may be nothing at all, no God, no justice, no purpose, only the white silence going on forever.

chapters.title: The Quarter-Deck
paragraphs: Captain Ahab keeps to his cabin for the first weeks of the voyage, and the crew begins to whisper. When he finally appears on the quarter-deck, he is a figure out of nightmare: a tall, gaunt man of fifty, with a face scarred and grim, standing on a leg made from the jawbone of a whale. Years before, on a previous voyage, a great white whale took his leg, and ever since, Ahab has lived for a single purpose.

One morning he summons all hands to the quarter-deck, and there, before every man aboard, he nails a gold doubloon to the mainmast with his own hand. The coin gleams in the sun. Then he turns to the crew and cries out his challenge: "Whosoever of ye raises me a white-headed whale with a wrinkled brow and a crooked jaw; whosoever of ye raises me that white-headed whale, with three holes punctured in his starboard fluke — look ye, whosoever of ye raises me that same white whale, he shall have this gold ounce, my boys!"

The crew stares, then understands. Every whaleman has heard of Moby Dick, the white whale that no harpoon can hold, the demon fish of a thousand stories. Ahab does not merely want to hunt him. He wants vengeance. He calls on each man by name, the mates and the harpooneers, and makes them swear. He passes around a great measure of grog, and the men drink, and their eyes burn, and one by one they join his oath. Even Starbuck, the good, God-fearing first mate, who protests that vengeance on a dumb brute is madness and blasphemy, is swept along.

Starbuck alone dares to answer back. He tells Ahab plainly that to be enraged with a dumb brute seems blasphemous, that he came to hunt whales for their oil and not to feed his commander's vengeance. Ahab's reply is the most famous speech in the book, and one of the most famous in American literature. All visible objects, he says, are but as pasteboard masks, and behind the mask of the white whale there lurks some unknown but reasoning malice. If man will strike, let him strike through the mask. How can the prisoner reach outside except by thrusting through the wall? To Ahab, the whale is not an animal but the wall itself, and he will batter his soul against it until one of them breaks.

Ahab's speech to Starbuck is the key to his soul. All visible things, he says, are only pasteboard masks, and behind the mask of the white whale lurks the unknown malice that rules the world. If man will strike, let him strike through the mask. It does not matter to Ahab whether the whale is truly evil or merely a beast. What matters is that his suffering must have a meaning, and the whale must pay. From this day forward, the Pequod is no longer a whaling ship. It is a weapon, aimed at a single white shadow somewhere in the vast Pacific, and every man aboard is bound to Ahab's quenchless feud.

That night, Ishmael lies awake and thinks about what he has witnessed. He has seen a sane and solemn oath turned into a madman's crusade, and he has sworn it too, caught up in the fire of the moment. He thinks of Queequeg sleeping peacefully beside him, of Starbuck's troubled face, of the gold coin gleaming on the mast. The voyage has changed. The hunt for oil and profit is over. The hunt for Moby Dick has begun.

chapters.title: The Three-Day Chase
paragraphs: For months the Pequod sails the world's oceans, following rumours and signs, and always the white whale stays ahead of them. They hear of him at the Cape of Good Hope, off Japan, in the Indian Ocean: ships stove, men killed, harpoons snapped like twigs. Ahab grows thinner and stranger, sleeping little, poring over his charts, communing with his shadowy Parsee servant Fedallah, who has prophesied that Ahab will die only when he sees two hearses, one not made by mortal hands, and that hemp alone can kill him. Ahab takes these riddles as promises of safety. He is wrong.

Fedallah, Ahab's strange Parsee harpooneer, has shadowed the captain like a second soul throughout the voyage, and his prophecies hang over the chase like a curse. He has foretold that Ahab will have no grave on land, that he will see two hearses upon the sea, the second not made by mortal hands, and that hemp alone can kill him. Ahab, hearing these riddles, takes comfort in them, for he cannot imagine how hemp could ever touch him, and he mistakes the prophecy's strangeness for a promise of safety. The reader, remembering Father Mapple's sermon about Jonah, feels a cold dread. Prophecies in great tragedies are never promises. They are traps.

On the first day of the chase, the cry comes from the masthead: there she blows! And there he is at last, Moby Dick, vast and white, rolling in the blue water, serene as a snow-covered mountain. The boats are lowered. Ahab stands in the bow of his boat like a figurehead of vengeance. But the whale is cunning and terrible. He smashes one boat with a flick of his tail, he dives and rises beneath another, and by nightfall the exhausted crews return to the ship, having touched the whale but never held him.

The second day is worse. Again the boats go out, again the whale toys with them, and this time Fedallah, the Parsee, is lost, lashed by tangled lines to the back of the great fish and dragged down into the abyss. Ahab watches his prophet die and still will not turn back. That night he works at his forge, tempering a special harpoon in the blood of the crew, and Starbuck begs him one last time to abandon the madness. Ahab refuses. He has gone too far to stop.

On the third day the sea is calm and the sky is clear, and the end comes swiftly. Moby Dick rises before them, and Ahab, standing alone in his boat, hurls his harpoon with all his remaining strength. The line sings out, the whale turns, and in a moment of terrible clarity Ahab sees his fate. The whale rams the Pequod, and the great ship, with all its crew, goes down in a vortex of white water. In the last instant, as the line catches him around the neck and drags him down, Ahab cries out his final defiance to the universe:

The destruction is total and almost silent. The great ship, which has carried these men across half the world, which has been their home and their fortress, shudders once and slides beneath the waves, taking with her every soul aboard except one. The boats are splinters. The masts are gone. For a moment the sea boils where she sank, and then the ocean smooths itself, indifferent as ever, and there is nothing left to show that the Pequod ever existed.
"Towards thee I roll, thou all-destroying but unconquering whale; to the last I grapple with thee; from hell's heart I stab at thee; for hate's sake I spit my last breath at thee."

And then there is silence, and then only Ishmael, floating on the open sea, clinging to Queequeg's coffin, which the faithful harpooneer had carved for himself and which now serves as a life-buoy. For a day and a night Ishmael drifts alone on the vast and empty ocean, the sole survivor of the Pequod, kept alive by the coffin of his drowned friend. At last another ship appears, the Rachel, still searching for her own lost sons, and she takes him aboard. Ishmael alone escapes to tell the tale, and his story ends where all great tragedies end: with the sea closing over everything, as if the Pequod and her crew had never been.

Far into the voyage, in the warm and windless waters of the tropics, Queequeg is struck down without warning by a violent fever. One morning he cannot rise from his hammock; by nightfall he is burning and raving, and the ship's surgeon can do little but shake his head. For days the great harpooneer lies helpless while the Pequod rolls on around him, and Ishmael keeps watch beside him, remembering the cold night at the Spouter-Inn when this same man climbed into bed with a tomahawk pipe between his teeth. Queequeg, who has faced whales and storms without flinching, looks at his own dying with perfect calm. He tells Ishmael, in his broken and dignified English, that he feels his end approaching, and that a man of his rank must prepare himself properly.

What he wants is a coffin. He sends for the ship's carpenter, a grave and obliging craftsman, and orders him to take his measure and build him a coffin shaped like a canoe, long and narrow, of the finest wood aboard. The carpenter sets to work with saw and plane, and Queequeg lies in his hammock and watches the box take shape plank by plank, as calm as a man ordering a new sea chest. There is no fear in him, only a kind of royal thoroughness. When the coffin is finished, he has it brought to his side, and with the last of his strength he climbs inside to try it, folding his great tattooed arms across his chest like a warrior laid out for burial.

Then, with the solemnity of a king arranging his tomb, Queequeg furnishes his coffin for the final voyage. He calls for his harpoon and lays it along his side. He asks for a small boat-paddle, for ship's biscuits and a flask of fresh water, and for his little black idol Yojo, which he sets upright near his head to keep him company on the way. He has the lid lowered over him to test the fit, and lies there in the dark for a time, trying his narrow house, before ordering it opened again. It is not despair that moves him but duty. A prince of Kokovoko must go to his fathers properly equipped, and Queequeg means to do the thing correctly.

But Queequeg's iron body refuses to die. Slowly, against every expectation, the fever breaks. The same immense strength that has hurled harpoons into whales and wrestled sharks on the deck turns against the sickness and drives it out of him. Within days he is sitting up; within a fortnight he is back at his post in the bow of the boat, leaner and quieter, but alive. He has looked death in the face, made all his preparations, and been dismissed for the present. The coffin, ordered for a corpse, is left without one, standing empty in the forecastle like a question no one can answer.

What does a man do with a coffin he no longer needs? Queequeg's answer is perfectly practical, and perfectly Queequeg. He has his spare clothes, his ditty bag, and his few small treasures moved into the long box, and the coffin that was meant for his burial becomes the sturdiest sea chest aboard the Pequod. The sailors grin when they see it, but no one dares mock him. There is something in Queequeg's quiet dignity that forbids laughter, and besides, every man aboard knows in his bones that his own chest might one day serve the very same purpose.

Then Queequeg does something stranger and more beautiful. Taking up his carving tools, he covers the lid of the coffin with the same mysterious hieroglyphics that cover his own body, copying the tattoos of his arms and thighs onto the wood, square by square, sign by sign, until the coffin wears his skin's own writing. No one aboard can read those markings. They are the written language of his island, a sacred script of gods and devils that died with the priests who taught it, and Queequeg himself can no longer say what every sign means. He knows only that they are his, that they tell his story in a tongue no living man can speak.

The crew regards the carved box with a mixture of awe and unease. The carpenter, proud of his handiwork, runs his fingers over the strange signs and shakes his head. The old sailors touch their charms when they pass it, half convinced it is bad luck to keep a coffin among the living, half convinced it is good luck to have cheated one. Only Queequeg is entirely at ease with it. He has done what his fathers taught him: he has made friends with death, furnished it, carved his name on it, and then, having settled the account, gone back to work.

Ishmael stands looking at the carved lid and feels the old mystery deepen around his friend. Here is a man carrying his own unreadable history on his flesh, and now on the box that was to have been his grave: a book no one can read, sealed in a coffin no one will use. The carved box takes its place among the sailors' chests in the forecastle, strange and silent, waiting through the long months of the hunt. Neither Ishmael nor Queequeg guesses what part it is yet to play in the story, or that the tattoos copied so carefully onto its lid will one day be the last familiar thing a drowning man clings to in an empty sea.

Ishmael finds himself returning again and again to the mystery of those carved signs. Queequeg's whole body is a text, and now his coffin is a second copy of it, and no one alive can read either one. The missionaries who taught him his few words of English never taught him to read his own skin. The priests of his island who could read it are dead, and the cosmology they guarded, the gods and devils mapped in blue across his prince's body, died with them. Ishmael realizes, with a pang, that his friend is a walking book in a language with no readers left, carrying his entire history into a world that can only admire the pictures.

And yet there is no sadness in Queequeg about any of this. That is the final wonder of him. He has taken the most terrifying object a sailor can imagine, a coffin, and made it familiar: measured it, furnished it, carved it, and turned it into furniture. The Christian sailors cross themselves at the sight of it; the pagan sleeps beside it in perfect peace. In the long war between man and death, Queequeg has won the only victory that matters. He is not afraid. And Ishmael, watching his friend stow his spare shirts in a coffin as calmly as another man would pack a trunk, begins to understand that courage was never about fighting. It was always about this: looking straight at the end and refusing to flinch.
chapters.title: Queequeg's Coffin

paragraphs: If Ahab is the dark soul of the Pequod, Starbuck is its conscience, and the two men are locked together like light and shadow. The first mate is a native of Nantucket, a long, thin, earnest man, a Quaker by birth and upbringing, and the only officer aboard who dares to speak plainly to the captain. His courage, Melville tells us, is not a hot sentiment but a practical thing, kept always at hand like a good tool, and beneath his steady seamanship there runs a deep natural reverence, a respect for the unknown that Ahab burned out of himself long ago.

Starbuck is the only married man among the officers, and his heart is half ashore. He carries the thought of his young wife and his little boy with him everywhere, like a weight in his breast that grows heavier as the voyage darkens. He signed aboard to hunt whales and earn an honest living for his family, not to feed one man's vengeance, and he is the only man who says so to Ahab's face. To be enraged with a dumb brute, he argues, is madness and blasphemy. A whale is an animal, not a devil, and no man's hatred can make it otherwise.

Ahab hears him out and sweeps him aside with that terrible speech about the pasteboard masks of the visible world, and Starbuck, outnumbered and bound by duty to his owners, yields. But yielding is not agreeing. Through the long months of the hunt, Starbuck keeps the ship running with flawless seamanship while his soul sickens within him. He does his duty to the owners who hired him, he obeys the captain he despises, and every order he carries out costs him something. He is a good man trapped in an evil voyage, and Melville never lets us forget the price of that entrapment.

There comes a night when the torment nearly breaks him. Ahab sleeps below, and Starbuck stands watch above with a loaded musket in his hand, and looks down at the sleeping tyrant, and understands with terrible clarity that a single shot would end the madness and save every soul aboard. He raises the weapon. His hand does not shake. And then, slowly, he lowers it. He cannot murder a sleeping man, even to save a ship, even to save himself. He walks away into the dark, and the moment passes, and the Pequod sails on toward its doom. It is one of the most quietly devastating scenes in the novel: the good man who had his chance and could not take it.

Late in the voyage there comes a day of unearthly beauty, the sea like glass, the air soft as a benediction, and Ahab and Starbuck stand together at the rail while the ship glides through paradise. For a moment the captain's iron seems to soften. He speaks of his forty years at sea, of the wife he has barely known, of the boy he can hardly remember, and something almost human moves in his scarred face. Starbuck seizes the moment and pleads with him: turn back, abandon the hunt, go home while there is still time. For one heartbeat it seems Ahab might listen. Then the shadow closes over him again, and the moment is gone, and Starbuck is left alone at the rail with the knowledge that nothing will turn this ship but the sea itself.

The crew knows Starbuck's worth, and loves him for it. The men would follow him anywhere, and in any other voyage he would have been the captain they adored. They see his troubled silences, they hear the strain in his voice when he repeats Ahab's orders, and they understand, without a word being spoken, that their first mate is suffering for them all. He is the proof aboard that ship that ordinary decency survived the madness, that a man could look straight into Ahab's hell and refuse to enter it, even while his duty chained him to the deck above it.

Starbuck writes no great speeches and performs no great deeds. His heroism is the heroism of endurance: showing up, doing the work, keeping the ship afloat, while the man above him spends them all like coin. He is the reader's stand-in aboard the Pequod, the one who sees clearly and is powerless, the one who knows the voyage is doomed and sails it anyway because his name is on the articles and his family is waiting in Nantucket. There are men like Starbuck on every doomed enterprise in history, and Melville honors him by making his suffering the moral measure of everything Ahab destroys.

He goes down with the Pequod on the third day of the chase, faithful to his post to the very last, the good man destroyed by another man's evil. His tragedy is in some ways more terrible than Ahab's, for Ahab chose his doom and Starbuck's was chosen for him. He is the novel's great might-have-been: the captain the Pequod deserved, the husband and father who should have gone home, the conscience of a ship that sailed without one. When the sea closes over him, it closes over the last decent man aboard.

There is a strange, unspoken respect between the captain and his first mate, and it makes Starbuck's tragedy sharper. Ahab knows exactly what Starbuck is: the better man, the honest sailor, the one the crew would follow into any sea. He needs him, and he knows he needs him, for no madman can work a whaleship alone. So Ahab handles Starbuck the way a man handles a dangerous tool, with a kind of wary admiration, giving him just enough authority to run the ship and never enough to challenge the hunt. It is the most backhanded compliment in the novel: Ahab trusts no one, and Starbuck is the one man he cannot do without.

In the great gales of the southern ocean, it is Starbuck who saves them all. While Ahab raves below over his charts, the first mate stands on the pitching deck through the blackest nights, reefing and steering by instinct, and brings the battered ship through seas that should have killed her. The men know it. They look to Starbuck in every crisis the way children look to a father, and he never fails them. That is the bitterest irony of his story: the man is a magnificent captain in everything except the one thing that matters, the power to say no to the madman who outranks him.
chapters.title: Starbuck, the First Mate

paragraphs: If Starbuck is the Pequod's conscience, Stubb is its laugh, and the ship needs him more than it knows. The second mate is a native of Cape Cod, a short, jolly, easygoing man who faces death with a pipe in his mouth and a joke on his lips, and nothing in heaven or earth seems able to rattle him. He kills whales cheerfully, eats his dinner cheerfully, sleeps the sleep of the untroubled, and meets even Ahab's blackest moods with an unshakable good humor that borders on provocation. Of all the mates, Melville calls him the oddest, and the most human.

Stubb's voice is one of the most distinctive sounds aboard the ship. He talks to the whales as if they were old acquaintances, chaffing them even as he drives the lance home, and he keeps up a running commentary on life that mixes a sailor's hard wisdom with a philosopher's shrug. When the crew is frightened by omens, Stubb laughs. When the wind dies and the ship lies becalmed under a burning sky, Stubb puffs his pipe and waits it out. There is something heroic in his refusal to be afraid, and something a little frightening too, as if his laughter were a wall built against thoughts he does not want to think.

Once, Stubb dreams a strange and troubling dream. He dreams that Ahab kicks him with his ivory leg, and that he, Stubb, furious at the insult, kicks back, and the two of them go hopping and kicking around the deck while the whole crew looks on. He wakes disturbed and tells the dream to Flask over breakfast, and Flask, solemn as an owl, offers learned interpretations, but Stubb shakes the whole thing off with a laugh. Yet the dream lingers like a prophecy in disguise. It is the only time anyone aboard, even in sleep, dares to kick back at Ahab, and it tells us what Stubb's waking humor conceals: a buried knowledge that the captain's authority has curdled into a kind of violence.

Flask, the third mate, is Stubb's opposite in build and in spirit. He is a short, stout, red-faced young man from Martha's Vineyard, and where Stubb is easy, Flask is eager. He regards the whale as an enemy made to be conquered, and he charges into battle with the fury of a prizefighter, as if every whale had personally insulted him and his honor depended on the kill. The sailors have nicknamed him King-Post, after the short, stout timber that braces a ship's frame, for he is built exactly like one: compact, sturdy, and made for hard knocks.

Flask's philosophy of life could fit on the blade of a harpoon. Whales were made to be killed, he believes, and he was made to kill them, and that is the whole of the matter. He has no doubts, no dark nights, no metaphysics. He goes at a whale the way a terrier goes at a rat, all courage and no questions, and his very simplicity makes him a perfect whaleman. Where Starbuck thinks too much and Stubb laughs too easily, Flask simply fights, and in the brutal, bloody work of the fishery, that is often exactly what is needed.

Each mate commands his own whaleboat, and each boat has its own harpooneer, and the three harpooneers are as striking as the officers they serve. Starbuck's harpooneer is Queequeg, the tattooed prince of Kokovoko. Stubb's is Tashtego, a tall, proud Indian of Gay Head, a born hunter with the sea in his blood. Flask's is Daggoo, a gigantic African nearly seven feet tall, with the bearing of a king and the strength of three men. Three pagan kings of the forecastle serving three Christians of the quarter-deck: the Pequod's boats are little floating worlds, each with its own character, rowing out together into waters where all their differences will mean nothing at all.

The three mates could not be more different, and that is precisely the point. Starbuck brings conscience, Stubb brings humor, Flask brings sheer fighting heart, and between them they represent every way a sane man can face an insane voyage: resist it, laugh at it, or throw himself into the work and think about nothing else. Melville, who shipped before the mast himself, knew that a whaleship runs on exactly this mixture, and he gives each mate his own unmistakable voice so that we hear the whole crew thinking aloud.

Together they are the machinery that makes the hunt work, and Ahab plays them like instruments. He gives Starbuck's conscience just enough rein to keep the ship sailing, he feeds on Stubb's good humor to keep the crew's spirits from breaking, and he aims Flask's blind courage straight at the whale like a loaded gun. They are brave men and good sailors, every one of them, and none of them can see that their virtues are being spent, day by day, in the service of a madness that will drown them all. That is the quietest tragedy aboard the Pequod: not that the mates are villains, but that they are not.

One black night, Stubb learns what it costs to cross the captain. Ahab is pacing the quarter-deck above, hour after hour, his ivory leg thumping on the planks like a death-watch beetle, and Stubb, trying to sleep below, finally snaps. He climbs on deck in his nightshirt to complain, sailor to captain, man to man, and Ahab turns on him with such concentrated fury that Stubb backs down the ladder without another word. The whole ship hears about it by morning. Even Stubb, the unshockable, the man who laughs at everything, has learned the exact dimensions of the captain's wrath, and he never jokes about Ahab again.

Watch the three mates together at the rail when a whale breaches far off, and you see the whole novel in miniature. Flask points and whoops like a boy, already tasting the fight. Stubb relights his pipe, grins, and makes a joke about the whale's table manners. Starbuck watches in silence, his face closed, seeing not a whale but another step toward the doom he cannot prevent. Three men, three philosophies, one ship. Ahab needs all three: Flask's hunger to drive the boats in, Stubb's humor to keep the crew from mutiny, Starbuck's skill to keep them all alive. He spends them the way other captains spend rope and canvas, and never once wonders what it costs.
chapters.title: Stubb and Flask

paragraphs: From the first days of the voyage, something is wrong aboard the Pequod, and the crew feels it before anyone can name it. On the night before sailing, shadowy figures are seen slipping aboard at Nantucket, and Stubb, keeping the anchor watch, catches glimpses of strangers moving silently in the dark between the masts. The white sailors whisper among themselves. Ahab says nothing at all. The ship sails with more men aboard than were ever signed on the articles, and no officer will say who the extras are or where they hide below.

The mystery breaks open far at sea, on the first day of real hunting, when Ahab's own boat is lowered away. At its oars sit five strange, silent men, dark-skinned and unknown to every sailor aboard, and standing in the bow is the most sinister figure in all of Melville's pages: Fedallah the Parsee. He is tall and gaunt, wrapped in white cloth, a great white turban crowning his head, and his eyes hold a fixed, unearthly stare, as if he were looking at something the rest of the world cannot see. He is a fire-worshipper from the East, and there is something phantom-like about him, as though he were less a man than Ahab's own shadow given flesh and set loose on deck.

From that day, Fedallah never leaves the captain's side. He stands near Ahab on the quarter-deck through the night watches, a pale shape beside the captain's dark one. He crouches in the maintop above Ahab's charts like a tiger over its kill. Some of the men swear he sleeps in Ahab's cabin; others swear he never sleeps at all. The crew comes to fear him almost as they fear Ahab himself, and Stubb, who laughs at omens and ghosts and the devil himself, does not laugh at Fedallah. There are whispers that the Parsee can read the future the way other men read the weather, and Ahab, who believes in nothing but his vengeance, believes in Fedallah.

For the Parsee has given his master prophecies, riddles wrapped in darkness. He has told Ahab that no grave on land will ever hold him, that only hemp can kill him, and that his pilot will appear before him at the very end. Ahab hears these strange sayings and takes comfort from them, for he cannot imagine how hemp could ever touch him, and he mistakes the riddle's strangeness for a promise of safety. The reader feels a cold dread creeping up the spine, for prophecies in great tragedies are never promises. They are traps, and Ahab is walking into his with his eyes wide open, led by the hand of his own phantom.

What makes Fedallah terrible is not any single deed but his perfect, reptilian stillness. While the rest of the ship rages and labors and sweats, he sits motionless, watching, waiting, like a fate that has already made up its mind and is simply biding its time. He is the only man aboard whom Ahab treats as something like an equal, and there are moments, in the small hours of the morning watch, when it seems the captain takes his orders from his shadow rather than the other way around. The two of them together on the lonely quarter-deck, the dark fanatic and the pale prophet, are the strangest pair ever to command a ship.

The white crew's terror of the Parsee grows with every week of the voyage. The sailors cross themselves when he passes, or touch their lucky charms, and the old superstitious hands among them whisper that no good can come of a ship that carries a fire-worshipper in secret. They are right, though not in the way they think. Fedallah brings down no curse from heaven. He brings something worse: certainty. He gives Ahab's madness the one thing it lacked, the conviction that fate itself has signed the hunting license, and a madman who believes heaven is on his side is the most dangerous creature on earth.

There is a sense in which Fedallah is not a man at all but a piece of stagecraft, Melville's way of giving Ahab's doom a face. Every great avenger in literature needs his familiar spirit, his Mephistopheles, his soothsayer, and Fedallah is Ahab's: the quiet voice that tells the tyrant exactly what he wants to hear, in words just dark enough to sound like destiny. He never raises his voice, never lifts a hand, never needs to. He simply stands beside the captain, pale and patient, and lets the prophecies do their work.

In the end, the riddles close around Ahab exactly as riddles do in every tragedy since the Greeks, fulfilling themselves in the one way he never imagined. The pilot appears. The hemp finds him. The grave that is not a grave receives him. And Fedallah, the prophet, goes down lashed to the very fate he foretold, as prophets in such stories always do. That is Melville's cruelest irony, and his most Shakespearean: the captain who thought the prophecies were armor discovers, too late, that they were the weapon all along.

The crew spins its own theories about the Parsee, each wilder than the last. He is a fire-worshipper from the ancient East, they say, one of the last of a dying religion, and that much is true enough. He crouches in the foretop for hours without moving, and the men aloft swear he is watching not the sea but something behind the sea. When Ahab must make a decision, he seeks out Fedallah first, and the two confer in low voices that no one can overhear. Whatever passes between them, Ahab always comes away with his jaw set harder. The prophet never talks the captain out of anything. He talks him into everything.

In the end, the two of them are not two men but a single doom walking the deck in duplicate. Ahab is the will and Fedallah is the warrant, the fanatic and the fate that certifies him. Melville understood something profound about tyranny: it always needs its prophet, its quiet validator, the still voice that turns one man's obsession into destiny. Without Fedallah, Ahab is merely a mad captain. With him, he is an instrument of heaven, or of hell, and no power on earth can turn him. The Pequod carries her own destruction aboard, not in the hold, but standing silent beside the man at the wheel.
chapters.title: Fedallah and the Secret Crew

paragraphs: Long before the Pequod ever sights him, Moby Dick is already the most famous whale in the seven seas. In every forecastle from Nantucket to the Azores, sailors tell and retell the stories: his enormous size, his wrinkled brow, his crooked and deformed lower jaw, the three harpoon holes punctured in his right fluke. They say his whole vast body is mapped with the scars of a hundred failed hunts, that he carries broken irons in his flesh like battle medals, and that no line ever made fast to him has held for long.

With each retelling the stories grow wilder. They say he has stove whole boats with a single flick of his mighty tail. They say he has taken the arms and legs of a dozen men, and the lives of more. They say he does not merely flee his hunters but turns upon them, hunting them in his turn with something like deliberation, something like malice aforethought. Some swear he cannot be killed, that he has been seen in oceans thousands of miles apart within days of each other, as if he could be in two places at once. Whether any of it is true hardly matters. By the time Ahab sails, Moby Dick is less an animal than a legend, a white ghost haunting the dreams of every whaleman alive.

The legend has a living prophet. On the docks of New Bedford, before the voyage begins, a ragged, half-crazy old man named Elijah attaches himself to Ishmael and Queequeg and croaks his warnings at them. He knows about Ahab. He knows about the missing leg. He hints at darker things still: at a captain who has sold his soul, at a voyage from which men do not return, at secrets hidden aboard the ship. Ishmael laughs the old man off, Queequeg stares in silence, and Elijah shuffles away into the cold, leaving his croaking prophecies hanging in the air like smoke. He is the novel's first warning bell, and almost no one hears it ring.

At sea, the Pequod falls in with ship after ship, and every meeting adds another stone to the legend. The captain of the Jeroboam tells of a mad prophet among his own crew who denounced Ahab as a blasphemer fleeing the wrath of heaven. Then comes the Samuel Enderby of London, and her captain, the cheerful Captain Boomer, shows the stump where his arm used to be, taken by the white whale, and begs Ahab to give up the hunt. Boomer speaks of Moby Dick almost with affection, as a noble beast that only defends itself when attacked. Ahab listens with contempt. To him these are not warnings but confirmations: the whale is real, he can be found, and he can be killed.

The legend is rooted in something real. Years before Melville wrote his novel, the whalers of the Pacific told stories of Mocha Dick, a huge white sperm whale off the coast of Chile who survived a hundred attacks and left a trail of wrecked boats behind him, and of the whaleship Essex, stove and sunk by an enormous sperm whale in the South Pacific, her crew set adrift to horrors beyond imagining. Melville knew these stories well. He took the white ghost of the sailors' yarns and the true terror of the Essex and forged them into something larger than either: a whale who is all whales, and more than a whale.

And so the great unanswered question of the novel takes shape, the question that divides Ahab from Starbuck and Ishmael from them both. Is Moby Dick a reasoning evil, a devil wearing a whale's body, as Ahab believes with all his broken soul? Is he merely a dumb brute, dangerous but innocent, as Starbuck insists? Or is he, as Ishmael sometimes dares to suspect in the small hours of the night watch, something stranger and more terrible still: neither good nor evil, but the blank, indifferent face of nature itself, wearing whiteness like a mask over nothing at all? The novel never answers. It only shows us, in the end, the men the question destroys.

That is the secret of the legend's power: the whale is a mirror, and every man who looks into it sees his own soul looking back. Ahab sees malice, because malice is what he brought with him. Starbuck sees a beast, because he refuses to see anything else. Ishmael sees a mystery, because mystery is the only honest answer he knows. Moby Dick himself, meanwhile, goes on being a whale, immense and white and unknowable, utterly indifferent to the meanings men hang upon him like harpoons.

For Ahab, the answer was never the point. Whether the whale is devil or beast or empty mask, Ahab will have his vengeance, and every story of the white whale's power is fuel poured on his fire. Each scarred flank, each broken harpoon, each drowned crew in the sailors' tales is, to Ahab, a personal insult demanding repayment. The legend has done its work perfectly: it has turned one wounded man's hatred into a holy war, and the Pequod sails on through the empty Pacific, following a ghost made of stories toward a reckoning made of flesh and blood and bone.

Ahab's hatred has a birthday, and the crew knows the story by heart. On a previous voyage, in these same southern waters, the white whale rose under his boat and took his leg with one snap of those deformed jaws, and Ahab lay for months in his bunk, raving and half-dead, while the stump healed into a scar that never stopped burning. When he walked again, it was on a leg carved from polished whalebone, and the men whispered that the whale was inside him now, literally part of his body, walking the deck on its own bone. Whether the story is true hardly matters. Ahab believes it, and that is enough to damn them all.

There is one more witness to the legend, and the strangest of all: Pip, the little Black cabin boy, the ship's drummer, who was once left alone in the open sea when his boat pulled away without him. They found him hours later, floating and singing, his mind gone. Now Pip wanders the ship in his madness, babbling wisdom that no sane man dares to speak, and Ahab, who despises every other soul aboard, treats the boy with an almost tender reverence. He keeps Pip near him in the cabin, as if the cracked mind of the child could see what whole minds cannot. In the Shakespearean economy of the novel, Pip is the fool, and the fool is always the one who tells the truth: that the hunt is madness, that the whale will win, that they are all already drowned men rowing.
chapters.title: The Legend of Moby Dick

paragraphs: Of all the wonders of the long whaling voyage, none is stranger or more beautiful than the day the Pequod falls in with the Grand Armada: a vast herd of sperm whales stretching to the horizon in every direction, thousands upon thousands of them, spouting and rolling as far as the eye can see. The cry goes up from the masthead, the boats are lowered in frantic haste, and the little craft row out into the midst of that living ocean, dwarfed and surrounded, like canoes lost in a stampede of mountains that breathe.

At first there is only chaos and terror. The startled herd begins to move, and the boats are towed at frightening speed through the churning white water. Lines tangle, oars clash, men shout orders that no one can hear. The whales wheel into a great circling mass, and the boats wheel helplessly with them, caught in a vast, slow whirlpool of living flesh. Ishmael, crouched low in his boat, looks around and sees nothing in the world but whales: backs like islands, flukes like falling trees, spouts like geysers, a wilderness of life closing in on every side, and he understands with a sailor's cold clarity how easily they could all be crushed like eggshells and never be missed.

Then, miraculously, the boat is drawn inward into the calm eye of the circling herd, and everything changes in a single breath. The water goes still as glass. The thunder of the hunt falls away. And Ishmael looks down through the clear green depths and sees what no landsman has ever seen, and few sailors: the secret heart of the whale world. Below him, in the sunlit water, swim the mothers with their calves, the young ones nursing, the babies rolling and playing like children in a meadow. It is a nursery, a cradle, hidden at the very center of the terror.

Ishmael gazes down, spellbound, at the tenderest sight in all of nature. The great cows hang motionless in the blue water while their young draw life from them. The calves nudge against their mothers and tumble over one another in play, innocent of harpoons and hunters and the whole bloody business of the fishery. Around them circles the outer ring of the herd, the bulls and the fighters, guarding the center with their mountainous bodies. It is a fortress built of love, a whole society arranged in rings around its most helpless members, and Ishmael, who came to murder them, can only stare in wonder at what he has stumbled into.

The spell cannot hold. A sudden panic ripples through the outer ring, the circle breaks, and the boats must dash for their lives through the boiling water, every man rowing for the ship as if the devil himself were at the tiller. The vision of the nursery vanishes astern, swallowed by spray and terror, but Ishmael carries it away with him like a secret wound. He has seen, in the very middle of the hunt, the proof that the whales are not monsters but mothers, not demons but families, and the knowledge sits in his heart like a stone beside his harpoon.

What haunts him most, in the nights that follow, is the contrast. An hour ago he looked down into a world of perfect peace, a floating Eden where the young were cherished and the strong stood guard over the weak. Now he is back in the world of Ahab, where every living thing is either a weapon or a target. The two visions cannot both be true, and yet he has seen them both with his own eyes. Somewhere between the nursery and the quarter-deck lies the whole meaning of the voyage, if meaning there is: that men can look straight at gentleness and still choose the lance.

The Grand Armada is Melville's great counterweight to Ahab's hatred, and the quiet moral center of the entire novel. For one luminous hour, the book shows us the whale world as it is when men are not killing it: ordered, tender, free, and complete without us. It is the story's silent argument against everything the captain believes, made not in speeches but in a vision vouchsafed to the humblest man aboard, and it stays with the reader long after the chase is done.

Ahab never sees the nursery. That is the final pity of it. While Ishmael gazes down into the clear water at the mothers and their young, the captain stands on the quarter-deck with his spyglass trained on the horizon, searching for one white shape among ten thousand, blind to the miracle beneath his own bows. The Pequod sails on through the Grand Armada and out the other side, and the peace it might have learned sinks back into the green depths, a glimpse of the world as it was before vengeance, which the ship, in its madness, passes forever without ever knowing what it has seen.

The boats come back aboard in an unusual silence. There has been no kill, no triumph, no bloody deck to scrub, and the men move about their work quietly, as if they had all seen something they cannot talk about. Even Stubb has no joke ready. Flask looks almost disappointed, cheated of his battle. Only Ishmael understands what has happened to them: they have looked into the clear water and seen the world as it was before men came with harpoons, and the sight has shamed them all without a word being spoken. It is the only victory the whales will ever win over the Pequod, and it is a complete one.

Ishmael will carry the vision of the nursery with him to the end of the voyage, and it will sit in his memory beside the whiteness of the whale like light beside darkness. He has seen two oceans now: the ocean of mothers, ordered and tender and complete, and the ocean of Ahab, where everything is prey. Both are real. Both are the sea. And the tragedy of the Pequod is that it sailed with a captain who could only see one of them, who looked down at ten thousand miracles and saw only the single white shape he had come to kill. The Grand Armada drifts astern, the mothers and calves sinking back into the green depths, and the ship sails on toward its appointment, having passed through paradise without ever knowing it was there.
chapters.title: The Grand Armada
